name: Forge
text:
**Decision: Build a single, modular "Core Package" first, then enrich tabs and draft elements from it.**

This keeps the first deliverable focused and reusable—like a toolbox everyone can borrow from. Starting with one solid package means we avoid wasted effort on duplicate work or half-baked elements. The trade-off is that we’ll move slower at first, but that speed bump pays off when the rest of the tabs and drafts snap into place cleanly. Quality first, always.

name: Vet
text: **Vet’s pushback:** The risk here isn’t just wasted effort—it’s *locking the team into a single package before we know what the tabs or elements actually need.* What if the "Core Package" ends up too generic to support the richer features later? The better alternative is to *build one minimal package for the first tab’s needs, then iterate*—that way, we test assumptions early instead of over-engineering a "toolbox" that might miss the mark. Settle it by prototyping the first tab’s core functionality in a week and seeing if the package holds up under real use.

name: Forge
text:
**Decision: Build the "Core Package" first, but with a strict "minimum viable" scope and clear extension hooks.**

This keeps us from over-engineering while still giving every future tab and element a shared foundation. The trade-off is that we’ll need to revisit the package later to add features—but that’s cheaper than refactoring a bloated, over-designed system. Starting small forces us to prove the package’s value before expanding it.
